It is April 16, 2026, so in my situation in Quzhou County I would keep the farm simple and stable. I would stay with the winter wheat and summer maize rotation because it fits the local climate, the land, the machinery, and my age. At 76, I would not want a labor-heavy or risky crop mix. With a high education level, I would still manage the field carefully, but I would focus on crops with predictable timing, mature seed supply, and a clear fertilizer and irrigation schedule. Winter wheat is already the backbone of the first half of the year here, and after harvest I would follow immediately with summer maize on the same land so the ground does not sit idle.

For wheat, I would use improved seed rather than traditional seed because I want stronger performance and more even stands without paying the higher management cost that comes with more specialized options. I would give it moderate but sufficient nitrogen, plus phosphorus and potassium to support rooting and grain filling. I would irrigate three times if water is available: once around jointing, once around booting or heading, and once during grain filling if the season runs dry. I would keep pesticide use limited and targeted, mainly for weeds and for disease or aphids if pressure appears. After wheat harvest, I would move quickly into hybrid summer maize because hybrid maize gives me the yield I want and it works well in the local summer heat. I would use no-tillage or very light disturbance after wheat so I can save moisture, reduce labor, and seed quickly. For maize, I would keep fertilizer somewhat heavier on nitrogen, irrigate twice if rainfall is not enough, and spray only when pest pressure justifies it. That is the plan I would choose because it balances yield, labor, and risk in a way I could manage confidently this year.
